name: Vultr
oneLiner: Global VPS provider: fixed-size virtual machines from $2.50 (IPv6-only) or $3.50 with IPv4, billed hourly with a one-hour minimum and a 672-hour monthly cap; a stopped server keeps billing until destroyed.
whatItIs: Vultr sells fixed-size virtual machines in 34 regions across six continents. Cloud Compute is the shared-CPU family: Regular Performance on older Intel and regular SSD, High Performance on current AMD EPYC or Intel Xeon with NVMe, and High Frequency on 3 GHz+ Xeon with NVMe. Every plan bundles vCPU, RAM, disk and a monthly egress allowance; there is no custom CPU/RAM split.

It is an ordinary Linux server product, not an agent sandbox. Root, SSH, any port, Docker if you install it, custom ISO boot, snapshots and block storage all work as on a normal VM. There is no prompt endpoint, no memory snapshot, no idle sleep, no per-second meter and no session limit; a server exists and bills until it is destroyed.

Above Cloud Compute sit Optimized Cloud Compute (dedicated vCPU: General Purpose, CPU Optimized, Memory Optimized and Storage Optimized), VX1 (newer dedicated plans with nested virtualisation), Cloud GPU and Bare Metal. This listing prices the shared Cloud Compute plans; the dedicated and GPU families are named where they change a verdict but are not in the calculator.
whoFor: People who want a real Linux server at a predictable monthly price in a specific region, and will run the OS, the agent and the backups themselves. The one-click Hermes and OpenClaw Marketplace apps make it a reasonable first VPS for a personal agent; the one-hour minimum makes it a poor fit for many short sandbox runs.
isolation: A full virtual machine per instance with its own kernel, disk and public IP: root, Docker inside, real SSH, custom ISO boot and any TCP or UDP port you open in the firewall. Outbound 25, 137–139 and 445 are blocked by default, and 1688 is blocked inbound only. Nested virtualisation is documented only on VX1 plans; GPUs are a separate product and Windows carries a licence fee.
sizes: Cloud Compute shared plans: Regular Performance 1–24 vCPU, 0.5–96 GB RAM, 10–1,600 GB SSD; High Performance and High Frequency 1–16 vCPU, 1–58 GB, 25–1,024 GB NVMe. Optimized Cloud Compute (dedicated) reaches 96 vCPU / 256 GB / 1,280 GB; VX1 reaches 192 vCPU / 768 GB. Extra disk is Block Storage, up to 16 volumes and 40 TB HDD or 10 TB NVMe per instance.

billing.model: Per-server hourly rate with a 672-hour monthly cap, plus separately billed Block Storage, snapshots, backups, object storage, reserved IPs, Windows licences and DDoS protection. Prices are USD; some regions differ and the console shows local pricing.
billing.meter: Hourly, with a one-hour minimum per server and a 672-hour monthly cap. The 2 vCPU / 4 GB plan is $20 a month and $0.0297619 an hour (the page rounds it to $0.03); 672 hours at that rate is $20.
billing.stopped: Nothing changes. A stopped server keeps its disk, IP and full bill until destroyed: "Servers that are stopped but not destroyed continue to incur hourly charges for reserved resources such as compute, storage, and IP address allocations."
billing.planFee: No plan and no fee. The monthly figure is a cap on usage: a server destroyed after 90 hours bills 90 hours at the hourly rate.
billing.minimum: No automatic signup credit. A Free Tier Program offers 1 vCPU / 512 MB / 10 GB in Miami, Seattle and Frankfurt to eligible applicants, and promo codes include a dollar-for-dollar deposit match up to $100. Paid servers need a payment method.

A.headline: $29.76 a month
A.shape: Regular Performance 2 vCPU / 4 GB / 80 GB, created and destroyed for each task

lines.label: Compute
lines.arithmetic: 1,000 servers × 10 min, each rounded up to 1 h = 1,000 h × $0.0297619

notes: The 2 vCPU / 4 GB plan is $20 a month; Vultr derives the hourly rate as $20 ÷ 672 = $0.0297619, and the pricing page rounds it to $0.03.
The one-hour minimum is per server, so 1,000 ten-minute tasks bill 1,000 server-hours, not 167.
One public IPv4 is included in the plan price; additional IPv4 addresses are extra.
The 80 GB plan disk covers the 10 GB asked for, and the 3 TB egress allowance covers any realistic agent traffic.
A.flag: This is the workload Vultr is worst at: a per-second sandbox bills the minutes used, while the one-hour minimum makes every 10-minute task cost a full hour.

B.headline: $40.00 a month
B.shape: Regular Performance 4 vCPU / 8 GB / 160 GB, 730 hours

lines.label: Compute
lines.arithmetic: 730 h × $0.0595238 = $43.45, capped at the $40.00 monthly price

notes: The 4 vCPU / 8 GB plan is $40 a month; 730 hours at the derived hourly rate is $43.45, so the monthly cap binds.
The 160 GB plan disk covers the 50 GB asked for.
The plan includes 4 TB of egress a month; overage is $0.01/GB.
Automatic backups would add 20%, about $8.00 a month.

C.headline: $20.00 a month
C.shape: Regular Performance 2 vCPU / 4 GB / 80 GB, 90 running and 640 stopped hours

lines.label: Compute
lines.arithmetic: 90 running + 640 stopped hours, billed to deletion: 730 h × $0.0297619 = $21.73, capped at $20.00

notes: Stopping does not stop the meter: a stopped instance reserves CPU, RAM, disk and IP and bills until destroyed.
The monthly cap binds because 730 billed hours exceed 672.
Snapshot-and-destroy is the only cheaper pattern: a 20 GB snapshot is $1.00 a month at $0.05/GB, plus 90 hours of compute at $2.68, but it loses the IP and the running state.
C.flag: Stopping does not stop the meter; a machine idle two-thirds of the month still pays the full monthly price.

facts.label: Founded and scale
facts.value: Founded in 2014; 34 regions, 80m+ instances deployed and 1.5m+ customers, with 75+ engineers.

source.quote: Vultr, founded in 2014, is on a mission to empower developers and businesses by simplifying the deployment of infrastructure via its advanced cloud platform.

facts.label: Ownership and funding
facts.value: Privately held. A December 2024 financing from LuminArx and AMD Ventures valued it at $3.5 billion; June 2025 added $329 million in credit financing.

source.quote: Secured $3.5 billion valuation in financing from LuminArx and AMD Ventures

facts.label: Certification
facts.value: SOC 2+ (HIPAA), ISO/IEC 27001:2022, ISO 27017, ISO 27018, ISO 20000-1, PCI Merchant and CSA Star Level 1.

facts.label: Status and SLA
facts.value: A public status page with JSON and RSS feeds, and a 100% uptime SLA on network and host-node availability, credited per service item on request.

facts.label: Data protection
facts.value: A GDPR DPA is available by request through an account manager or support ticket; Vultr acts as processor for customer content.

source.quote: Yes, Vultr offers a Data Processing Addendum (DPA) to support customers that are subject to the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)

well: An always-on agent on a small machine: 2 vCPU / 4 GB / 80 GB for $20 a month, or 1 vCPU / 2 GB / 55 GB for $10, with 2–3 TB of egress included.
A coding box for one developer: 4 vCPU / 8 GB / 160 GB for $40 a month, with the repository safe on the disk between sessions.
A one-click Hermes or OpenClaw on a real VM with root and a public IPv4, from the Marketplace, at the plan price with no app surcharge.
Global placement: 34 regions including nine in the EU, with free anycast DNS and a static public IPv4.
Anything that needs a real kernel, root, Docker, arbitrary ports or a stable public IP.
badly: Bursty work: a stopped server bills exactly like a running one, so a three-hours-a-day agent costs the same as a 24-hour one.
Many short runs: every server is billed at least one hour, so 1,000 ten-minute tasks cost 1,000 hours.
Outbound allowlisting: Vultr's firewall filters only incoming traffic; egress control is a host firewall you run.
Live resizing down, memory snapshots, idle sleep, per-second billing or a hard user-set spend cap.
One-click apps that ship a default password: change it before exposing the instance.

usability.dashboard: Yes: the Vultr Console creates instances, block storage, snapshots, backups, VPCs, firewalls, reserved IPs, DNS and object storage, with usage graphs and invoices.
usability.withoutCode: Partly. Marketplace one-click apps (Hermes, OpenClaw, Docker, Coolify and others) deploy from the console, but everything after that — the model key, the channel, TLS, the database — is terminal or app configuration.
usability.signup: Email plus a payment method (card, PayPal, Alipay, UnionPay or crypto). New accounts start with an account credit limit that is raised on request; the free tier is a separate application.
usability.docs: Extensive docs at docs.vultr.com with product guides, a full API v2 reference, an official CLI, a Terraform provider and official Go, Python, Node, PHP and Ruby clients.
tripsUp: Powering a server off does not stop the bill; only destroying it does.
The minimum billing unit is one hour, so a ten-minute task pays for sixty minutes.
The hourly rate on the pricing page is rounded; Vultr's own billing FAQ derives it as monthly ÷ 672, and the API publishes a third figure for some plans.
The firewall filters only incoming traffic; outbound rules are yours to run inside the VM.
The Hermes and OpenClaw Marketplace apps print a default password (Password) in their listings.
Windows licences are extra: $16–$384 a month on top of the plan.
Prices can differ by region; the console shows the local price.
Resizing is upgrade-only; downgrades are unsupported.
Outbound ports 25, 137–139 and 445 are blocked by default; open a ticket to remove them, while a few ports are permanently blocked.

caveats.issue: A stopped server is not a paused server
caveats.detail: There is no pause, sleep or hibernate. A stopped instance keeps its disk and its IP but also its full bill; the documented way to stop paying is to destroy it, which permanently deletes the data.

caveats.issue: The one-hour minimum punishes short runs
caveats.detail: Usage is billed in whole hours per server, so any task under an hour costs a full hour: 1,000 ten-minute tasks bill 1,000 server-hours, not 167.

caveats.issue: Three first-party hourly rates for the same plan
caveats.detail: The pricing page shows $0.03/hr for the $20 plan, the billing FAQ says the hourly rate is the monthly rate divided by 672 hours ($0.02976), and the public plans API returns $0.027. The card uses monthly ÷ 672, the figure the billing FAQ defines, so the 672-hour cap equals the monthly price. A reader using the page's $0.03 would get $30.00 for workload A instead of $29.76.

evidence.quote: The hourly rate is determined by dividing the monthly rate by 672 hours (28 days).

caveats.issue: One-click apps ship a default password
caveats.detail: The Hermes and OpenClaw Marketplace listings both print a username and the password "Password" in their getting-started steps. An instance exposed before that password is changed is trivially accessible; the OpenClaw app also includes a browser VS Code terminal with the same password.

caveats.issue: The free tier is an application, not a tier
caveats.detail: The Free Tier Program offers one 1 vCPU / 512 MB / 10 GB instance in Miami, Seattle and Frankfurt, granted on a randomized, weighted basis to applicants. It is not a standing allowance for every account, and paid servers still need a payment method.

strengths: $20 a month for a real 2 vCPU / 4 GB / 80 GB server with 3 TB of egress and a public IPv4.
34 regions, nine in the EU, with free anycast DNS and static IPs.
One-click Hermes and OpenClaw apps on a normal VM, with no agent surcharge.
A full API, official CLI, Terraform provider and SDKs in five languages.
SOC 2+ (HIPAA), ISO 27001/27017/27018/20000-1, PCI Merchant and a 100% uptime SLA.
Block Storage, File System and S3-compatible Object Storage as first-class products.
